noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: explain how alveoli are adapted for gas exchange by diffusion between air in the lungs and blood in capillaries

primer.text: You have seen the respiratory system's layout; now zoom to the business end. Each alveolus is a microscopic air sac wrapped in capillaries, and everything about it — shape, walls, moisture, blood flow — exists to make oxygen and carbon dioxide swap places as fast as possible.

lessons.title: Alveoli Built for Diffusion
lessons.opening: Gas exchange happens between the air in an alveolus and the blood in the capillary wrapped around it, and every alveolar feature sharpens that swap. Rounded sacs in huge numbers give an enormous surface area; the alveolus and capillary walls are each a single flattened cell, so the diffusion gap is tiny; a film of moisture lets the gases dissolve before crossing; and constant ventilation plus a brisk blood supply keep the concentration gradients steep on both sides.
keyPoints: Many rounded alveolar sacs create a very large surface area for exchange.
Alveolus and capillary walls are one cell thick, keeping the diffusion distance minimal.
A moisture layer lets gases dissolve before they diffuse across.
Ventilation refreshes the alveolar air, keeping oxygen high and carbon dioxide low inside.
A good blood supply sweeps CO2-laden blood away and delivers oxygen-poor blood, maintaining gradients.

low.restatement: Large area, thin walls, moisture and fresh air give the alveolus its speed.
low.analogy: A busy border crossing with many booths (area), short queues (distance) and fast traffic both sides (gradients).
low.examPointer: List all the adaptations together — exam answers want the full set, not one.

medium.restatement: The alveolus stays imbalanced on purpose so diffusion never slows.
medium.analogy: Two crowds on opposite sides of a gate, both regularly refreshed, keep people flowing through.
medium.examPointer: Pair each adaptation with the word gradient — most marks live in that link.

check.stem: Why do alveoli have thin, single-cell walls?

options.text: To minimise the distance gases must diffuse
options.explanation: A short path makes each exchange fast.
Surface area comes from the many rounded sacs, not the wall thinness.
Warmth plays no role in this adaptation story.
Defence is not what the thin wall is for.

check.stem: What maintains a high oxygen concentration in the alveolar air space?

options.text: Ventilation — fresh air brought in by breathing
options.explanation: Each breath replaces used air and tops up the oxygen.
Moisture helps gases dissolve; it does not refresh the air.
Wall thinness shortens the path; it does not renew the air.
Area scales the exchange; only ventilation refreshes it.

check.stem: Why is a good blood supply essential for gas exchange?

options.text: It keeps delivering CO2-rich, oxygen-poor blood to maintain the gradients
options.explanation: Fresh arrivals keep both sides of the wall imbalanced.
Warming is not the capillaries' exchange role.

options.text: Because blood pressure flattens the walls
options.explanation: Pressure does not shape the gradient story here.

options.text: To store oxygen inside the alveoli
options.explanation: Blood carries oxygen away, not into storage.

check.stem: What role does the moisture layer play?

options.text: Gases dissolve in it before diffusing across the wall
options.explanation: Dissolving is the first step of the crossing.

options.text: It traps dust before it reaches the blood
options.explanation: Dust trapping belongs to the upper airways' cilia and mucus.
Area comes from the sacs' rounded shapes.
Cooling is not the moisture layer's job.

check.stem: Which feature gives the alveoli their very large surface area?

options.text: The great number of rounded sacs
options.explanation: Many small spheres pack in more area than one large cavity.
Thinness is about distance, not area.
Moisture serves dissolving, not area.
Pleural membranes surround the lungs, not each alveolus.

check.stem: Name the site where gases are exchanged between lung air and blood.
State four adaptations of the alveoli for gas exchange.
check.modelAnswer: Large surface area, one-cell-thick walls, a moisture layer, and good ventilation with blood supply to keep the gradients steep.

check.stem: Explain why the concentration gradient at the alveolus would flatten without ventilation.
check.modelAnswer: Because exhaled air lingers: oxygen would be used up and carbon dioxide would accumulate in the alveolar space until it matched the blood's levels, and with no difference between the two sides diffusion would stop — ventilation prevents that by renewing the air.

check.stem: At altitude the air holds less oxygen per breath. Use the alveolar adaptations to explain why climbers breathe faster.
check.modelAnswer: Thinner air lowers the oxygen side of the gradient, so the alveolus must be refreshed more often to keep even that reduced gap steep; faster breathing raises the renewal rate, compensating for the poorer air with more ventilation per minute.

glossary.definition: A microscopic air sac at the end of the bronchioles; the lung's gas exchange surface.
The difference in gas levels between two sides; the driving force of diffusion.
The breathing cycle that refreshes air in the lungs.
